analysis.one_liner: Makes drug makers pay Medicare a rebate when their prices rise faster than inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 2 cosponsors in October 2019 and died in committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require drug manufacturers to pay Medicare a rebate on any Part D drug costing $100 or more per person per year whose price rose faster than inflation since 2016 (or since the drug first hit the market for newer drugs). Manufacturers that refused to pay could face a penalty of 125% of the owed rebate and could lose Medicare coverage for their drugs. The money would go back into the Medicare trust fund. The bill was referred to two House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries who use high-priced drugs, and taxpayers, who fund Medicare drug coverage through premiums and general revenue. If manufacturers pay rebates, some of that cost pressure eases, and the threat of rebates gives manufacturers a reason to hold prices closer to inflation.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers must pay CMS a rebate equal to the number of units dispensed times the amount by which the drug's average manufacturer price exceeded inflation since 2016, or since the drug's first year on the market for drugs approved after 2016, for covered Part D drugs costing $100 or more per person per year.
A manufacturer that fails to pay faces a civil money penalty of 125% of the rebate owed, and keeping Medicare coverage for the drug requires the manufacturer to have a rebate agreement in effect.
Rebate payments are deposited into the Medicare Prescription Drug Account in the Federal Supplementary Medical Insurance Trust Fund, returning money to the program that covers seniors' drugs.

The bill includes limits aimed at gaming: line extensions of existing single-source drugs are covered by a formula tied to the original drug, and the Secretary can waive rebates during drug shortages.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers, whose prices have risen faster than inflation, would owe rebates that reduce their revenue on Medicare's biggest-selling drugs.

drawbacks.text: The bill covers only Medicare Part D, so people with private insurance or no insurance get no direct benefit from the rebates.

Drugs approved after 2016 are measured against the price in their first year on the market, so a manufacturer that sets a very high launch price never owes a rebate on it — only later increases are penalized.
The bill bars judicial review of the unit counts, the determination of which drugs qualify, and the rebate calculation, leaving manufacturers no court challenge on those numbers.
The rebate applies only to drugs whose average cost to a plan runs at least $100 per user per year, so price increases on cheaper drugs go unrebatable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The mechanism is a proven one — Medicare already imposes inflation rebates on drugs in Part B, and this extends that idea to the much larger Part D benefit. It would return real money to Medicare and give manufacturers a direct financial reason not to raise prices faster than inflation. Its main design weakness is that it polices price increases but not launch prices, so a new drug could debut at a very high price with no rebate owed. It is a targeted fix rather than a comprehensive drug-pricing overhaul, but its costs fall almost entirely on the manufacturers driving the problem.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee in October 2019 and sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on October 8, 2019, with Reps. Brian Higgins and Susan Wild as cosponsors — the only cosponsors it ever attracted.
The same day, it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, and shortly after to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee.
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a committee vote, was never reported to the House, and never reached the floor before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers are better off: no rebate obligation was created, and drug prices in Medicare Part D continued to face no inflation-based penalty during that Congress.

for.name: Jan Schakowsky
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited its only two cosponsors.

for.name: Brian Higgins and Susan Wild
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, the only two members to do so.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee and Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committees of jurisdiction (with the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral in October 2019 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Brand-name pharmaceutical industry
against.what_they_did: Consistently opposed inflation-rebate requirements on Medicare drugs during this period, and no member of either party moved the bill forward.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, and with only two cosponsors and no vote ever taken, the record shows no partisan contest to measure.

industries.note: The bill would force manufacturers of high-priced drugs to rebate to Medicare every dollar their prices rose faster than inflation, plus a 125% penalty for nonpayment. Their interest in blocking it ran directly against seniors' drug costs and the Medicare trust fund.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare drug plans
industries.note: Rebates would flow to the government rather than through plan negotiations, marginally changing the rebate dynamics plans and PBMs live on, but the bill does not directly regulate them.
